title: Inverse-type CoOx-TiO2 catalysts for the Energy-Efficient Thermo-Photo Valorization of CO2
abstract: In this research, composite catalysts based on mixtures of titanium and cobalt oxides were synthesized and tested in the thermo-photo reduction of carbon dioxide. The cobalt loading varied between 2% and 8 M %, providing an outstanding activity in the selective production of carbon monoxide through the reverse water gas reaction. The sample doped with 4% Co optimized catalytic performance, with an excess over the photo and thermo alone processes above 27 % and an energy efficiency of 1.1 %. These values indicate that the sample displays the top performance reported so far. A physico-chemical characterization of the catalysts was also carried out showing that nearly amorphous cobalt (II) oxide entities are embedded within nanocrystalline anatase nanoplatelets within an inverse-type configuration. The use of in-situ infrared provides conclusive evidence that the promotion of the catalytic performance under dual excitation is intimately linked with the formation and evolution of formate-type species at the catalyst surface. A novel dual-excitation catalytic process using novel composite CoOx-TiO2 catalysts would open new ways for the energy-efficient elimination and valorization of carbon dioxide.
paragraphs: A huge number of industrial activities generate carbon dioxide (CO2) as the main and currently undesired primary product. The use of fossil fuels in engines and machines, or the steel and concrete industries are examples of energy intensive applications emitting greenhouse molecules, particularly carbon dioxide. In recent years, growing concern about climate change has led to the search for solutions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions which are steadily increasing in the atmosphere and have serious consequences for human health and the environment (). Among numerous ways to solve the problem, catalysis plays a crucial role as not only can provide a tool to control the emission of the target molecule(s) but also can generate simultaneously valuable products and contribute to the settlement of a new circular economy (; ).

Catalytic reduction of CO2 is one of the processes with prime importance in generating industrial-relevant products from such molecule. As carbon dioxide is a rather stable molecule with relatively limited interaction with the majority of the catalytic solids, (; ) the implementation of reductive ways to activate the C–O bond requires sufficient energy inputs and adequate and well-engineered catalysts. Thermal, photo or electro catalytic processes haven been implemented in this search. Yet the optimization of the efficiency of the process as well as the control of the catalytic properties concerning activity, stability and selectivity would appear as open questions requiring scientific and technological efforts to drive progress in the field (; ). Integration of two energy sources in a single chemical process has shown potential to address these two issues, particularly to increase the efficiency of the process. Within this field, thermo-photo catalysis has emerged as a promising approach in the conversion of CO2 into valuable products, such as carbon monoxide as well as many others, methane, methanol, formic acid and others (, ). Thermo-photo catalysis attempts to combine heat and light sources into a single process and its application recently expanded to numerous catalytic fields among which degradation of pollutants, ammonia synthesis, hydrogen production as well as carbon dioxide transformation can be highlighted (). In all cases, successful catalysts trigger the synergistic combination of the two energy surfaces along the reaction path. Yet a positive enhancement of activity has been only reported for a relatively low number of catalytic formulations active under single thermal or phonic excitation (; ; ). In addition, even successful (thermal, photo or thermo-photo) catalysts do not provide a single product in the above mentioned catalytic processes, with the consequent loss of efficiency and competitiveness (, ; ; ; ). To highlight the significance of these challenges for the thermo-photo reduction of CO2, we note that, to the best of our knowledge, the highest reported energy efficiency is below 1 % (). In addition, high activity is frequently reached with limited selectivity towards a single product (; ; ; ).

In this work, we developed an inverse-type cobalt-promoted titania-based materials working within a highly selective thermo-photo transformation of carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide. Aside from other things, inverse (composite) catalytic formulations have been developed to increase the stability of the solids under reaction conditions by controlling the sintering of active phases or, more generally speaking, to limit morphological changes by strong contact between components (). To date, this technology has not been applied for the preparation of cobalt-promoted titania-based materials. Note, on the other hand, that the Reverse Water Gas Shift (RWGS) reaction (CO2+H2 → CO + H2O) and thus the selective production of carbon monoxide, is of great interest, as CO can be used industrially for the synthesis of a wide variety of compounds, being those involved in the Fischer-Tropsch process the most relevant (, ). In the RWGS reaction, both components of the CoOx-TiO2 catalyst play active roles. In a simple approximation, titania is central for light handling phenomena while the cobalt-containing component plays a key chemical role in carbon dioxide activation and evolution (; ).

In this contribution, we will show that the intimate contact between the two components of the inverse-type CoOx-TiO2 composite generates a rather interesting system, with catalytic performance significantly improved with respect to previous published cobalt-promoted titania-based materials. The mentioned enhancement would consider energy efficiency issues, well below 0.5 % for the already studied systems, as well as activity and selectivity, particularly the latter, as carbon monoxide has been always obtained together with methane (; ). Moreover, the use of in-situ infrared spectroscopy will unveil key chemical information to interpret catalytic performance under single and dual excitation conditions.

The synthesis procedure to provide a careful contact between the components and adequate morphological properties for our CoOx-TiO2 systems is outlined in Fig. 1. An inverse microemulsion method is used. First, an organic phase was prepared with n-heptane, Triton X-100 as surfactant and hexanol as co-surfactant. After stirring this solution, Co nitrate was added (in different amounts depending on the desired Co content of the solid) and precipitated using tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMH). Following this step, Ti isopropoxide was added to the solution. The hydrolysis of the isopropoxide takes place in the aqueous micelle and allows to obtain a Ti-containing precursor surrounding the Co precursor (as depicted schematically in Fig. 1). This resulting mixture was left stirring overnight to be centrifuged the next day and washed with methanol. After that, it was left for 12 h drying at 100 °C and calcined at 450 °C for 2 h. Samples were named as TixCo where x is the molar content of Co with respect to Ti. This parameter was explored from 3 to 8 mol. %.

Basic characterization was performed on the obtained catalysts. Chemical composition (cation content) was measured using inductive couple-plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES; Optima 3300DV PerkinElmer spectrometer, USA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), UV–Vis spectroscopy (UV–Vis) to know the bandgap of the materials, and Brunauer-Emmet-Teller adsorption isotherms (BET). A Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer with Ni-filtered Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 Å) was used to acquire XRD patterns. UV–visible spectra were obtained using a Varian Cary300 apparatus (USA) with the help of a Teflon film as a reference. Catalysts were degassed overnight at 140 °C to test morphological properties using nitrogen physisorption (Micromeritics Tristar-II 3020 equipment, USA).

Further examination of the catalysts was carried out using other techniques, photoluminescence (PL), scanning and transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and temperature programmed desorption (TPD). PL experiments were carried out using an excitation line of 365 nm and a Horiba FluoroMax Plus (Germany) Fluorescence Spectrophotometer. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was carried out using a 200 KV JEOL STEM/STEM 2100. The microscope was equipped with an energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS) to evaluate the composition. For the TEM histograms approximately 30 images of each sample were evaluated to study the particle size and morphology were representative. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were taken using a JEOL F-6335 microscope (JEOL Ltd., Tokyo, Japan), operating at 15 kV. Before, the scaffolds were mounted on stubs and carbon coated under vacuum using a Quorum Q150T Carbon Coater. XPS data were acquired using a SPECS® spectrometer (UK). The spectrometer is equipped with a PHOIBOS® 150 WAL hemispherical energy analyzer, an XR 50 Al-X-ray source and a μ-FOCUS 500 X-ray monochromator. To appropriately correct for potential charging effects, the binding energies (BE) were referenced against the C 1s peak (284.6 eV). The CASA 2.3.25 program was utilized for fitting procedures which uses a Shirley background (). TPD experiments were carried out using a home-made U-shaped reactor and a TCD detector. Samples were treated with CO2 at 50 °C up to saturation, cleaned with nitrogen for ca. 30 min until stable baseline and, finally, a temperature rump of 10 °C min−1 applied.

Finally, infrared spectroscopy was utilized to interrogate the samples under in-situ conditions and obtain information of the activation and evolution of the reactants at the catalyst surface. In-situ Diffuse reflectance infrared spectroscopy DRIFT was carried out using a Bruker Vertex 80 FTIR spectrometer. Samples were pre-treated with nitrogen for 15 min before measurements were carried out at the reaction conditions described in the next subsection. Spectra were obtained at dark (or thermal-alone) and illuminated (photo or dual thermo-photo excitation) conditions at selected temperatures. At each step of the experiments, the signal was recorded for ca. 40–45 min until lack of changes was noticed. The spectrum obtained under nitrogen atmosphere, taken immediately before the catalyst is contacted with the reaction mixture, is used as background for all experiments.

For the measurement of the activity, the catalyst has been distributed homogeneously on a pyrex glass tube. Inside this tube, we placed a compensated resistance which will allow to step-up the temperature of reaction. On the outside there is another tube of the same material concentric to the first one, which will allow the passage of gases between both in contact with the catalyst. A scheme of the reactor is presented in Fig. S1 of the supporting information section. The light source is provided by four lamps arranged symmetrically around the reactor. A mixture of CO2, H2 and N2 (10 mL min−1) will enter the reactor as a carrier, with a CO2:H2 ratio of 1:1. 13C labeled carbon dioxide, supplied by Sigma-Aldrich (99% purity), were used in selected experiments. The gas output of the reactor was analyzed by means of a gas chromatograph (Agilent GC 7890) and a mass spectrometer (OmniStar 300). The reaction has been tested at different temperatures between RT and 350 °C and at all temperatures with and without light. Full details of the experimental step-up, including light and heating sources, gas handling and environment, reactants/product detection systems and reaction procedures are detailed in the supporting information section.

The activity was quantified using the reaction rate (r), measured following recommendations of the IUPAC (). The procedure is fully detailed in the supporting information section. Rates under thermal-alone (denoted by the T suffix), photo-alone at room temperature (P suffix) and thermo-photo (TP suffix) were measured. To obtain a measurement of the synergy between the two excitation sources, several parameters were calculated (). First, an excess rate (re) was calculated according to equation (1).(1)re=rTP−(rT+rP)

The excess rate was expressed as a percentage over the rTP parameter. The quantum efficiency of the reaction was also calculated in order to obtain information about the use of photons under reaction conditions. This in turn requires measuring and obtaining the local superficial rate of photon absorption and considers thermal effects on optical properties as detailed in the supporting information section ().
Finally, the global energetic efficiency of the process is measured using equation (2).(2)ρ(%)=rΔHreactionAWs·100

In this last equation, r is the rate of the reaction (mol s−1) and ΔHreaction is the standard enthalpy of the reaction. Note that the RGWS is an equilibrium, and this affects the calculation of the denominator of equation (2). Details of such calculation are presented in the supporting information section. Finally, the Ws parameter corresponds to the total energy supplied by the dual excitation per surface area unit (W m−2) and A is the surface area of the catalyst ().

Fig. 2 summarizes results concerning the basic physico-chemical characterization of the composite catalysts. The XRD diffractograms of the samples display the characteristic pattern of the anatase polymorph of titania ((JCPDS card 21–1272; I41/amd space group) (). This occurs for all samples, irrespective of the cobalt content. Raman spectroscopy confirms the dominant presence of the anatase phase, without detecting peaks associated with any other crystalline phase (). Thus, both techniques provide evidence of the exclusive presence of anatase as a (nano)crystalline phase at the catalysts under study.

The nanostructured nature of the anatase phase becomes evident by the width of the XRD and Raman peaks. In fact, using the Scherrer equation and the XRD patterns, () we measured an anatase primary particle size of ca. 9–10 nm for all samples (Table 1). The catalysts obtained after calcination have mesoporous nature in all cases, showing a characteristic H2(a) type hysteresis loop. A representative example is included in Fig. 2. Results for other samples are presented in Fig. S3. Results concerning the BET surface area and average pore volume of the catalysts are collected in Table 1. High surface area materials are obtained after the calcination step. The (bare) titania reference displays a BET surface area of ca. 145 m2 g−1. The presence of cobalt on the composite catalysts triggers an increase of the surface area. The BET surface area of the CoOx-TiO2 composite samples takes values in the 170–180 m2 g−1 interval. As the primary particle size of the dominant component of the catalysts (anatase) also increases modestly from the corresponding bare anatase value (Table 1), this ca. 20 % increase detected in surface area values indicates that the cobalt component favors the mesoporosity of the samples. This is likely an effect of the synthesis procedure, as the cobalt nuclei are synthesized before the occurrence of the titania precursor hydrolysis. The presence of such nuclei affects the stacking of the anatase particles on the solid(s) and, consequently, the morphology of the samples (Fig. 1 and Fig. S3). This ends up with the production of a mesoporous materials having cobalt species (partially) surrounded by titania species. Note that, according to the ICP-OES analysis, the cobalt content of the materials is the nominal one within a 3.8 % of error in the whole interval explored (2–8 mol. %). The absence of any cobalt-related XRD-Raman signal, would indicate a limited dimensionality of the corresponding cobalt-containing entities and/or some kind of amorphization. This is further discussed below.

After calcination, the optical properties of the solids were investigated with the help of UV–visible spectroscopy (Fig. 2). The titania reference presents the characteristic decay at the region of ca. 400 nm, typical of a semiconductor with a gap into the UV region. Considering that anatase is an indirect gap semiconductor, () the band gap energy is calculated as 3.06 eV for this sample. The presence of cobalt changes the shape of the spectrum at the gap region as well as produces localized features typical of oxidized Coδ+ species above ca. 600 nm (). The band gap energy shows a constant value of 2.52 ± 0.03 eV for all composite catalysts (Table 1). Due to the absence of significant changes in the XRD patterns and Raman spectra (Fig. 2), this indicates a strong interaction between the cobalt and titania components, with the absence of any doping of the anatase structure by cobalt species.

A SEM/TEM study of the materials was also carried out to complete the morphological-structural characterization of the materials. The SEM micrographs for selected samples are presented in Fig. S4. Cobalt appears to display a homogeneous dispersion for all solids. As mentioned, the preparation method uses the cobalt entities as centers to nucleate titania. This would favor the homogeneous dispersion of the cobalt component on the final catalysts (Fig. 1). More information about the different components of the composite catalysts can be deduced from the TEM analysis. Fig. 3 displays results for the Ti4Co and Ti6Co samples and Fig. S5 for the Ti2Co and Ti8Co samples. Nanosized entities, characteristic of the ca. 10 nm titania platelets, are clearly visible in the high magnification micrographs (Fig. 3 and Fig. S5). Darker entities correspond to cobalt containing entities which are essentially amorphous according to the absence of electron diffraction patterns. The cobalt-containing particles appear always surrounded by titania entities, as schematically depicted in Fig. 1. The average primary particle of the cobalt-containing component grows from ca. 7–8.5 nm in our series of composite samples. Although the particle size distribution is relatively broad in all cases, the corresponding distributions have a limited growth of the average primary particle size with the cobalt content. This would point out the above mentioned strong interfacial contact between the two components of the composite systems.

The characterization of the initial stage of the catalysts is further investigated with the help of the XPS study of the powders. Fig. 4 collects XPS results from the Co 2p region for the composite samples. Rather similar spectral profiles can be observed in Fig. 4A for all samples. The Co 2p3/2 signal peaks at ca. 780.0–780.1 eV in all cases. This binding energy points out the existence of Co(II) species in an oxidized environment (; ). The strong shake-up satellite at near 6 eV from the main Co 2p3/2 peak is also characteristic of the CoO type entities (; ). The stabilization of Co(II) entities on titania with a local CoO-type structure has been previously described as a result of a strong interaction between the two components (). Interestingly, the Co/Ti XPS ratio (Fig. 4D) displays a nearly linear relationship with the Co content of the materials. This fact is in agreement with the smooth increase of the primary particle size observed using microscopy and thus the relatively minor effect of this parameter on the Co/Ti XPS ratio, which is dominated by the Co content of the powder. As a summary of the characterization results, we note that the composite catalysts would thus contain nearly amorphous CoO-type entities surrounded and protected by nanocrystalline anatase platelets. This inverse-type configuration is a consequence of the preparation method and favors the interaction between components.

The reaction rates obtained for photo (room temperature), thermal-alone and thermo-photo conditions are presented in Fig. 5. This figure displays the reaction rate of CO formation, the single product formed with selectivity above 99 % in all cases. Note the logarithm scale of the rate axis. Switching 12C/13C labeled CO2 experiments under pseudo-stationary conditions provided evidence that carbon monoxide comes out from carbon dioxide (Fig. S6). The samples can be divided into those having relatively low activity, bare titania and Ti2Co, middle, Ti8Co, and high activity, Ti4Co and Ti6Co. Samples along the series display reaction rates differing up to three orders of magnitude at the same testing conditions. Although the samples show (photo)activity at room temperature, the output is rather small when compared with thermo-alone results using temperatures in the 150–350 °C interval tested. In fact, for all samples, differences above two orders of magnitude are visible in Fig. 5 between the thermo (at optimal temperature) and photo alone values of the reaction rates. Interestingly, the activity of the samples under dual thermo-photo conditions shows a marked dependence on the cobalt-content of the catalysts. This can be easily visualized with the help of the excess rate parameter (equation (1)). The evolution of this parameter through the samples, expressed as a percentage over the value of the thermo-photo rate, is presented at the bottom panel of Fig. 5. Positive effects on activity are encountered for the Ti4Co and Ti6Co samples while none or negative effects (depending on temperature and catalyst) can be observed for the Ti2Co and Ti8Co samples. The rates of the Ti4Co and Ti6Co catalysts reach values from 1 to 2.2 mmol g−1 h−1 for temperatures equal or above 250 °C. The quantum efficiency reaches a maximum of 3.3 × 10−2 % for the Ti4Co sample. As the quantum efficiency parameter measures the rate of the reaction per mol (Einstein) of photon absorbed, the same behavior of the rate and quantum efficiency parameters (both presenting maximum values for the Ti4Co/Ti6Co catalysts) indicates that the differences observed in optical properties among samples (including band gap energy) are not critical to interpreting the optimization of the activity under dual excitation. Compared to the (room temperature) photo-alone result, the quantum efficiency increases by 155 times. Moreover, the overall efficiency of the process shows a value of 1.1 %. This value is among the highest presented in the literature (; ; ). The last parameter can be the best choice to compare with literature reports as the reaction rate of photon-related processes is a parameter with a strong dependence on the measurement conditions (flow or batch condition, temperature, photon intensity, etc.) and the quantum efficiency only informs about the photon-related part of the efficiency under dual excitation (; ). Therefore, considering the efficiency parameter, the maximum reported in the literature is, to our knowledge, 0.83 % (). This corresponds to a lower value than the one here obtained. We would like to remark that this excellent performance is obtained with a nearly 100 % selectivity to CO. The last fact can be highlighted as the cobalt containing thermo-photo catalysts typically display the simultaneous production of several products for the CO2 reduction (; ; , ). In the case of CO, the best samples show maximum selectivity in the 80–90 % range (; ; ).

Comparing the thermo-alone and thermo-photo behavior shown in Fig. 5, it can be noted (see the excess rate) that the optimum enhancement under dual excitation takes place at 250 °C. To interpret this fact and, in general, the thermo-photo behavior of the samples we first analyzed the catalyst(s) stability under reaction. This was jointly carried out with the analysis of the charge handling capability and CO2 adsorption capability of the samples together with the interrogation of the reaction mechanism using in-situ infrared spectroscopy. The stability of the Ti4Co catalysts under thermo-photo conditions was tested at the mentioned 250 °C temperature. Fig. S7 shows results for a test in the continuous mode of operation over nearly 120 h. The stability of the catalyst as well as the reversibility between thermo-alone and thermo-photo conditions are both evident. Note that the stable catalytic performance occurs in the presence of (a limited amount of) water produced during the RWGS reaction. This would come out, in first place, from the structural-morphological stability of the materials. As can be observed in Table 1, the main physico-chemical properties of the catalysts lack any variation between pre and post-reaction samples. Furthermore, the XPS results collected in Fig. 4 also demonstrate that the cobalt oxidation state does not suffer changes under reaction conditions. The Co/Ti XPS ratio (see Co 2p signal presented in panels B and C of Fig. 4) also lacks any significant modification under all (thermo-alone and thermo-photo) reaction conditions tested here. The joint consideration of the post-reaction (physico-chemical) characterization results would thus indicate the rather good stability of the catalysts in terms of structural, morphological and relevant electronic (optical, oxidation state) properties of the solids.

The PL of the samples under UV illumination was examined. As well known, the PL spectrum of pure anatase is dominated by two de-excitation events. These two types of annihilation events correspond to the commonly called green and red regions, roughly below and above ca. 475 nm (see Fig. S8). They correspond to electronic decay transitions joining localized and band-type states as band-to-band de-excitation has negligible probability due to the indirect nature of the semiconductor gap (; ). The presence of cobalt has a strong effect on the PL signal, increasing the probability of green-type transitions and decreasing the red ones for loadings below 6 mol. %. For the highest 8 mol. % cobalt content, the PL spectrum changes, and a general decay of intensity is observed with respect to the bare titania reference sample. The most important point to note here is the lack of correlation between (the behavior through the series of catalysts) of the PL (Fig. 6) intensity and catalytic activity (Fig. 5) observables. As a lower PL intensity is related to a decrease on the charge recombination process, (; ) the comparison of the mentioned two parameters indicates that charge recombination is not a key issue to interpret the behavior of the dual-excitation catalytic properties through the series of CoOx-TiO2 composite samples.

TPD experiments were also conducted to test the influence of cobalt on the CO2 adsorption capability of the solids. Fig. 6 displays results considering the temperature programmed desorption of the molecule. Titania is known to have a moderate adsorption capability for carbon dioxide (; ). Fig. 6 provides evidence that cobalt affects this capability. Although the total quantity of carbon dioxide absorbed only changes by a modest 15 % throughout the samples of the series, a strong effect on the stability of the molecule can be detected. The latter is easily visualized in the fitting results presented in panels B and C of Fig. 6. As customary carried out, desorption peaks can be classified into low, middle and high temperature. For our purposes, as the promotion of the dual thermo-photo activity is maximized above ca. 200 °C, we focused the analysis on the middle and high temperature peaks appearing above this cut-off in Fig. 6. As can be observed in panel D of Fig. 6, there is a strong effect of cobalt with respect to the bare titania reference. A decrease in the quantity of the strongly adsorbed species, stable at and above ca. 250 °C, is detected. Such an effect appears more pronounced as the cobalt content of the catalyst increases. This behavior clearly indicates that, at relevant reaction temperatures, cobalt will decrease the interaction of carbon dioxide molecules absorbed at the surface of the composites solids, allowing them to be highly mobile at reaction temperatures. However, no apparent correlation between the promotion of the activity and the corresponding quantity of adsorbed carbon dioxide at the catalyst surface (at reaction temperatures) would come out from Fig. 6D. So, although important at thermal (and of course photo) conditions, the potential effects of cobalt on the surface coverage of the carbon dioxide do not seem to contribute significantly to the enhancement of activity observed under dual excitation.

Rather insightful results are nevertheless obtained if compared the infrared spectra acquired under reaction conditions for different temperatures of operation under photo (room temperature), thermal (dark conditions from room temperature to 350 °C) and thermo-photo (dual excitation at 250 and 350 °C) conditions. Results for a sample having essentially no “dual-source” promotion of activity (Ti2Co) and the one presenting the maximum of the promotion (Ti4Co) are shown in Fig. 7, Fig. 8, respectively.

For the Ti2Co sample, at dark conditions and room temperature, Fig. 7 provides evidence of the evolution of relatively somewhat broad and ill-defined bands at 1300–1325, 1590 and 1692 cm−1. The high wavenumber band may be assigned to the activated carbon dioxide species (•CO2−) while the other bands would indicate the presence of several carboxylate type species (; ; ). All these bands appear insensitive to the illumination of the catalyst. Under this last condition, a new band at 1186 cm−1 appeared and would indicate the formation of bridged carbonates (). The presence of carbonates appeared to be promoted at 250 °C, with the formation of additional monodentate carbonate species (1082 cm−1) (; ; ). In the infrared spectra taken above room temperature, the negative band at ca. 1650 cm−1 corresponds to the desorption of water. At the highest temperature tested, 350 °C, the presence of hydrogen-carbonates would be pointed out by the band at ca. 1433 cm−1 (; ; ). The most important point to interpret the activity under dual excitation is the absence of changes under dark and illuminated conditions for the temperatures of operation above room temperature. This would indicate the absence of differences in surface species and rationalize the lack of an enhancement of activity under dual excitation for this sample.

For the active Ti4Co catalyst, the results of the infrared study are collected in Fig. 8. At dark conditions, a broad band at 1300-1325 cm−1 is observed with rather weak ones among which the 1691 cm−1 appeared the most significant. Considering the previous discussion, the surface of the catalyst would be able to activate the carbon dioxide molecule with formation of the •CO2− and carboxylate species. For our purposes, the most interesting result takes place when the solid is heated at 250 °C. This temperature corresponds to the one of maximum synergy under dual excitation. Under dark conditions rather weak and ill-defined peaks can be observed, however, the illumination of the sample triggers the formation of well-defined and intense bands at 1355, 1376 and 1582 cm−1. The three bands are indicative of the presence of formate species at the surface (; ). Note that the formate moieties appeared exclusively under illumination. At higher reaction temperatures, 350 °C, we only detected a broad band at 1098 cm−1 (monodentate carbonates ()) which are insensitive to the dark/illumination conditions. The results would thus point out that the specific formation of formate species are responsible of the enhancement of activity under dual excitation in the temperature region around 250 °C.

So, as a summary of the in-situ infrared study, the technique allows to demonstrate that the promotion of a formate-based route would justify the outstating thermo-photo catalytic properties of the Ti4Co sample. The combination of the in-situ infrared analysis and characterization results allows to interpreting activity, particularly the synergistic effect taking place under dual excitation (see Fig. 9). Initially, light absorbed by the solid, mostly by the titania component, generates electron-hole pairs. The embedded, amorphous-like CoOx particles efficiently capture holes and produce protons from the hydrogen molecule. Note that our systems contain near amorphous CoO-type entities and not metallic Co nanoparticles. The capture of holes can be favored by the Co(II) 3d orbitals energetically located near anatase valence band and is promoted by the intimate contact between phases (). As previously discussed in the literature, a two electron activation route would take place first with the electronic activation of the carbon dioxide molecule, followed by the hydrogenation of the moiety to generate a formate type intermediate, which would in turn decompose to produce carbon monoxide (; ). The comparison of infrared and TPD results provides evidence that the activation of carbon dioxide (leading to the formation of •CO2− species under dual excitation) would not be strongly correlated with the activity behavior through the series of samples and that the evolution of such (activated) species is key to promote catalytic properties under dual excitation. Thus, as previously discussed in this section, differences in the series of samples concerning both light-handling properties as well as the (thermo-photo) activation of the carbon dioxide molecule appear of little relevance to justify thermo-photo activity.

The combination of heat and light strongly promotes the evolution of carbon dioxide through the formate-type reaction path over others and is thus responsible of the synergistic effects observed in the catalytic performance of the active Ti4Co sample under dual thermo-photo conditions (Fig. 9). On the contrary, the exclusive use of thermal activation promotes to a higher degree a carboxylate route (with accumulation of this intermediate at the surface) which triggers the generation of a significantly lower quantity of hydrogen. This route, with specific details connected with the particular carbonate species formed by each sample, is also characteristic of poorly active thermo-photo samples (see, as an example, the results presented in Fig. 7 for the Ti2Co catalyst) The summary of the multi-technique analysis can be visualized using the scheme presented in Fig. 9. According to this figure, for active thermo-photo samples, we can infer that the cobalt species are able to facilitate the interaction of protons (previously formed in this component) with the activated •CO2− species. This may be promoted by local structures where the intimate contact between titanium and cobalt oxide components takes place.

Composite CoOx-TiO2 catalysts were prepared using a single pot microemulsion procedure. An embedded nearly amorphous Co (II) oxide phase surrounded by anatase nanoplatelets in an inverse-type configuration was obtained after calcination for cobalt molar contents up to 8 %. The corresponding solids display high surface area and an intimate contact between components. The catalytic behavior of the solids in the reduction of carbon dioxide under dual thermo-photo excitation showed a strong dependence on cobalt content. The most interesting CoOx-TiO2 catalysts showed a stable (over ca. 120 h of operation) and high selective (to CO) catalytic response. Moreover, synergy between thermal and photonic sources was observed for the catalysts having a 4–6 molar % of cobalt. The most active system showed an energy efficiency of 1.1 %, being this the largest reported in the literature.

To interpret the synergy under dual excitation we analyzed the implication of the charge handling properties of the solids as well as the carbon dioxide adsorption and activation at the catalysts surface. The use of in-situ infrared provided conclusive evidence that the synergistic effect observed under dual excitation comes out from the promotion of a formate-type intermediate and its subsequent decomposition to yield carbon monoxide. The combined thermo-photo effect promotes the hydrogenation of the activated carbon dioxide surface moieties in a way that cannot be achieved by the simple sum of the two energy sources. For the Ti4Co case, the ration rate parameter shows an excess value over 27 %. So, the inverse-type combination of cobalt and titania oxides shows potential to open the way to an innovative dual-excitation catalytic process for the energy-efficient elimination and valorization of the carbon dioxide pollutant.
